items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: But it was great to have a chance to work with them.

ctx.x: Okay. On June 6th, 1957, a date entitled Free and Easy, Jackie and Roy accompanied by the Bill Holman orchestra. You‟ve done other sessions with at least Jackie Cain, but on this one were both Jackie and Roy [Kral]. You have both arranging and conducting in addition to being your bands. Jackie and Roy at that point were enjoying a great deal of popularity, if I recall correctly. Was this beneficial for you, as far as your career as well?

No. It kept me eating for a few months. In other words, it supported me for a while. A funny thing about that: Roy was really in love with Lou Levy‟s harmonic – the changes he used, and substitutes. So he came up with this idea where – what was it? – he would give sketches to Lou, and Lou would harmonize them. Then I would write – what he thought was, I would write the chart. But the way it was that Lou harmonized it, and there were figures in there. So I more or less orchestrated the thing, plus adding some of…
Tough in that regard, insofar as that process.

items.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998
items.q: And Bill Holman did a couple of vocalese things.

ctx.x: Ralph Burns wrote the ballads. And it was really nice.
And Bill Holman did a couple of vocalese things.

Bill Holman did two. And so it was a fun album for us because it got us out of doing the same thing, and you know you like to change what you’re doing. It makes it more interesting, more exciting. And so when we did that Ernie Wilkins wrote the arrangement and at the end he changed it. He thought it would be more effective for a record. Because it’s easy to do a fade out.
